headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: ECC can read/write shared files and use MCP, while awesome-selfhosted is a non-executing knowledge list with no isolation guarantees.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is a knowledge-management list with no I/O surfaces, but ECC can read files, use MCP, and treat files/skills as workflow inputs. If content from the list is copied into ECC or shared via files, prompt-like instructions could be misread. The pathway is interaction-based, not inherent to awesome-selfhosted alone.
conditions: IF content from awesome-selfhosted is copied into ECC-managed files or MCP inputs
IF ECC parses imported text as instructions or skills without provenance checks
mitigations: Keep awesome-selfhosted content read-only and outside ECC workspaces
Disable MCP ingestion for imported list content
Add a provenance header to copied snippets
Review any imported text before placing it in ~/.claude or ~/.cursor/ecc

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-selfhosted itself touches no data classes and has no network egress, but ECC reads and writes local files, session state, and MCP configs, and can call external APIs. If the pair shares a workspace, ECC can expose copied content or metadata beyond the local boundary. The risk is moderate because the leakage depends on shared files, not default behavior of the list.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or copied notes
IF sensitive material is stored in files ECC can read or upload
mitigations: Separate the awesome-selfhosted notes from ECC work directories
Remove secrets from any shared markdown or config files
Restrict ECC network egress to approved destinations only
Audit ~/.claude and ~/.cursor/ecc for sensitive content

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-selfhosted has no write capabilities, but ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, install packages, and spawn subprocesses. If both are used in the same repo or directory, ECC can overwrite or mutate artifacts that the list references or that operators expect to remain stable. Uncertainty about orchestration and locking pushes this to high.
conditions: IF ECC and the list are maintained in the same git checkout or shared directory
IF ECC runs without external locking or a separate root
mitigations: Place ECC in a separate working tree
Use git locks or a single-writer policy
Make the awesome-selfhosted source read-only during ECC runs
Snapshot the repo before ECC edits

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is a curated reference, and ECC has a strong tool-use surface plus session/skills machinery that can operationalize imported content. If ECC treats copied recommendations as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into incorrect installs, config changes, or security findings. The pair does not prove automation, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF ECC consumes recommendations from awesome-selfhosted without verification
IF those recommendations are converted into commands, installs, or config edits
mitigations: Require human review before executing imported recommendations
Tag imported items as unverified in ECC
Use a checklist to verify sources before actioning them
Limit ECC to drafting, not executing, changes

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or retention mismatch is documented for awesome-selfhosted, and ECC mainly exposes local session/config surfaces plus GitHub/App integrations. The pair does not show a concrete compliance breach path from the profiles alone, so only a low residual risk remains. The other agent is cited because the only plausible compliance exposure would flow through ECC's storage and API surfaces.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into ECC session files or MCP configs
IF ECC uploads that regulated data to external services
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of ECC-managed files
Review retention settings before use
Disable unnecessary API integrations
Store compliance-sensitive notes in a separate vault
